en: As though pricked in a gland,
Semetey leaped up.
The reason he leaped up:
All his earliest forefathers were khans,
Blessed by Khizr from their origins,
The offspring of that accursed one.
All his first ancestors were khans,
Blessed by Khizr from the beginning,
The offspring of that scourge.
Who greased the river valleys,
When enmity broke out,
Who slew even his own kin,
The offspring of that one doomed to burn.
Who poured blood into clear water,
Those who incurred his wrath,
Who seized and slew them,
The offspring of bloodthirsty Manas.
Wherever he had spent the night,
An enduring holy shrine arose.
Favored by Khizr from his origins,
Dumbuku Manas tribe,
The more he was extinguished, the more he smoldered;
The more he died, the more he flourished,
The offspring of commanding Manas.
Perhaps you have heard:
His first ancestor was Tuboi Khan,
After Tuboi came Boyon Khan,
Boyon Khan's wolf,
And after him Chayan Khan.
Descended from Chayan Khan,
After him came Bala Khan.
Bala Khan's son,
The paragon of Muslims,
After him came Ogoi Khan.
Let me tell you about Ogoi.
They clad him in blue-steel armor.
Wielding a mottled blue shield,
They came saying, 'I shall meet him,'
And many enemies were made to crawl.
From Ogoi Khan came Karakan,
Who broke through gorges and made roads,
Who attacked many lands.
From Karakan came Khan Zhakyp.
From that ill-intentioned unbeliever—
Perhaps you have heard—
From that dark, gray-maned hero,
Born and grown great in Altai,
The enemies who challenged him were destroyed.
At eight he sprang into action;
When he reached nine,
Blood flowed from those who opposed him;
The news of him drove souls out.
When he reached ten,
He broke into courts and took spoils.
When he reached twelve,
Those who faced him perished;
Those who met him crawled.
His fame was known among the people.
'Manas will unleash his wrath,' they said.
In the khagan of Beijing's
Register he was inscribed.
His father Manas had risen as khan;
His terrible might drove souls out.
When Manas came from Altai,
His fathers and forefathers
He used to gather wonders,
And destroyed Alooke.
Manas's son, the rascal,
The fierce one who took after his father—
Then the boy said:
"Taking a great army from you,
What desire would I fulfill?
My considered words are these:
Let me move away myself.
Leaving Bukhara and taking the road,
Taking an army worth the whole world,
Would I act against myself?
Would I slaughter my own people?
Grandfather, who would listen to these words of yours?
Let a dark, dug grave listen!
Do not ruin my purpose;
Do not speak such words!
Who should hear these words of yours?
Let a dark night hear them!
When I am in Talas,
When I arrive safely and settle,
I shall grow strong and refreshed.
When horses grow fat and fit,
When men grow stout and powerful,
When the marrow bones fill with fat,
When the young men's hearts are at ease,
When the people move up to higher ground,
When summer comes,
When I arrive safely and settle,
When I have grown strong and fully refreshed,
I shall not stand idle.
I shall gather the peoples of the world!
Grandfather, to you yourself
I shall send six swift horses;
I shall send a palm-sized letter.
Not only Bukhara—I myself
Shall gather the whole world.
Upon the damned Chinese
I shall wage a mighty war.
If you want a spectacle, see it then!
I shall rout and drive their army.
The Chinese Kongurbai with the prominent nose—
If I find the chance, I shall kill him!
I shall not launch a holy war now.
I shall not take the army you have chosen.
The Kyrgyz people left by my father—
With an army taken from you,
I shall not bring havoc upon them!
When I consider it, grandfather,
Should I take the army you have chosen,
And the honored, numerous Argyn people
Slaughter them myself?"
Manas's son spoke thus,
Telling the people stern words with forethought.
He was no longer a child.
As he stood, no longer a child,
His grandmother Korpozhan
Said to Temir Khan:
"This only son of Manas,
The numerous people left by his father Manas—
He will surely go to them," she said.
"The dear child we gained when dying—
If you do not heed his command,
If you do not give him what he wants,
Lest he plunder the valuables,
Lest he wreak havoc on everyone,
Lest he put an end to you all!
Your khojas in white turbans,
Your mullahs who read their lessons,
Your elders with words like Luqman's,
Treating you all as worthless,
Lest he slaughter you together,
Lest he put an end to you thus!
Lest he bring strife upon Bukhara,
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
Your beauties who sway as they walk,
Lest he beguile and take them as booty!
In red dresses, with spear-slim waists,
With swaying, ribbon-slim waists,
Lest he take your daughters as booty,
And drive them away to the Kyrgyz,
Lest he put an end to you all!
He has become a glowing ember.
In our prosperous Bukhara,
There has been no such wild one.
He imprisoned the wandering dervishes,
He beat the mendicants.
When he saw a khoja, he kicked him,
And shut him in his mosque.
When they saw his wild deeds,
All who heard with ears and saw with eyes,
All the people grew weary.
To the orphan going to his homeland,
If you do not give a full inheritance,
Will he not slaughter the foolish people?
You are a man stingy with livestock.
If you let your miserliness seize you,
Will God not suddenly strike you?
Heed what I say.
To Manas's orphan son,
Grant every wish!
Upon Aktulpar,
Load gold and silver.
To Manas's orphan son,
Bring it out and offer it.
Full of valor and courage,
Your little one, the Bloodthirsty One's son,
For twelve years
You kept from knowing of his father;
You concealed it from him.
Consider this terrible thing:
He bears a grudge on that account.
Preparing seventy red single-humped camels,
Braid each tail.
Let no grudge remain within him.
Load gold and precious metal by the pood,
And give it to this orphan!
I have more words, more to say.
Again, my khan, heed me!
Forestall the quarrel;
Send him on his way without offending him!
His mother, wretched Kanykei,
Made trouble when she was a girl,
Shook the world and unsettled the people.
As a married woman, that fierce one
Shook conventions and unsettled the people.
His mother is a fierce, unmanageable hero;
His father Manas is an exceptional lion.
You should heed my words.
If you do not heed my words,
Your people in the city of Bukhara
You will plunge into a desolate night.
Again, my khan, hear my words!
When I came to make a household with you,
I bore twelve daughters in all.
After those twelve daughters,
Female only in name,
I bore a lion like Kanykei.
Semetey, born of Kanykei,
Is no stranger or outsider,
No child to regard as foreign.
That's a lot of lies,
I spent a lot of time alone,
Your protector, born of your own flesh,
The Aktulpar you speak of
Has become a troublesome, cherished horse.
Because of that winged steed,
Your twelve sons-in-law became estranged.
I have words to say another way:
When she came to her birth family, you would not give it.
Kanykei bears a grudge.
You are a khan stingy with livestock;
You are an ill-intentioned man.
Heed what I say.
For the orphan, beyond a mere horse,
Get him a wife!
If you do not perform this service,
If you do not gather these people,
Lest he slaughter them all,
Lest he put an end to you all.
If you think about it,
He is your spring flowing through a valley,
Your grandchild born of your child,
Your lamp found when you were dying.
You took him while still green and tender;
You made him your child."
His grandmother spoke thus,
And brought his grandfather, the khan, to his senses.
Ill-intentioned Temir Khan,
She brought the man to his senses.
Then Temir Khan said,
"If he is moving away, let him go.
Let him reach his people safely."
His heart was deeply troubled;
Tears poured from his eyes.
Then Ysmayyl and Koloy wept together:
"While Semetey was here,
Our darling orphan,
We hoped he would be our support.
From this Bukhara,
My darling orphan,
Take whatever you choose!
Ask caravan merchants for news,
And toward unfortunate Bukhara,
Cast your eyes from time to time.
Of your grandfather and mother's brother,
'Are they truly safe and well?' ask,
And seek news from time to time."
The numerous people of Bukhara—
After their khan had spoken thus,
